passage:
Subject: I said something today

Dear Meghna,

You know Uday, the quiet one on the accounts desk? In today's review Mr Bose blamed Uday for the late report, though the delay was because sales sent the figures at 6 pm on Thursday. I have the email timestamps. My stomach was in knots. Then I put my hand up and said, "The figures reached us Thursday evening. I can show the emails." Two others nodded. Mr Bose went quiet, then said we would look at it again. I'm not sure it will fix anything, and I'm a bit scared I've marked myself. But silence would have told the whole floor that this is normal. Uday just said "thanks" in the pantry and looked at the floor. Wish me luck?

Pallavi

qa.q: What did Pallavi have that showed why the report was late?
Why is Pallavi scared even after speaking up?
qa.a: Pallavi worries that speaking up may have marked Pallavi as trouble, even though silence felt worse.

qa.q: What made Pallavi's speaking up safer than a bare accusation?
qa.a: Pallavi used facts, the emails with timestamps, and two others nodded in support.

qa.q: How might Uday have felt after Pallavi spoke?
qa.a: Probably relieved but awkward, since Uday said only "thanks" and looked at the floor. 🙂

grounding: Pallavi speaks up with facts when a coworker is blamed unfairly, aware of the risk and that silence makes injustice normal.
